subject: The Hyatt Regency Kansas City walkway collapse, 17 July 1981. Two suspended walkways hanging over a crowded hotel atrium fell during a Friday-evening tea dance, killing 114 people - at the time the most devastating structural collapse in United States history. The federal investigation (NBS Building Science Series 143, May 1982) found the cause was the box beam-hanger rod connection. The connection as drawn already failed the Kansas City Building Code. Then, during shop-drawing review, the original single continuous hanger rod was replaced with two interrupted rods, which doubled the load the fourth-floor connection had to carry - 20.3 kips became 40.7 kips, against a code-expected ultimate capacity of 68 kips and an actual capacity of 18.6 kips. No one recalculated it. Three parties stamped the drawing. In 1985 the Missouri Administrative Hearing Commission found the engineer of record and the project engineer guilty of gross negligence, defined as conscious indifference to a professional duty, and in January 1986 the Missouri Board revoked their licences - the first American engineers to lose their licences for gross negligence. No one was ever criminally charged.
central_question: A change was made to one detail on one drawing, and everybody in the chain assumed somebody else had checked it. What does it take, and who has to answer, when that is the whole reason 114 people die?
viewer_promise: By the end the viewer can do the arithmetic themselves: they will understand exactly what a hanger rod, a box beam and a nut do, why hanging the lower walkway from the upper one doubles the load at a single connection while changing nothing else, why the original design was already illegal but would still have held that night, and why a state licensing board decided that the responsibility for checking is not something an engineer is allowed to delegate.
surprise: Three of them. (1) The change did not weaken anything - the steel, the welds and the workmanship were all found sound. It simply doubled what the same steel was asked to carry. (2) The walkway that survived was the weakest of the three: NBS found that without the change, the third-floor walkway would have been the most critical, and it still had a high probability of failure during the life of the building. (3) Two years before the collapse the atrium roof fell in during construction, the firm was paid an additional fee to check every connection in the hotel, reported 'we then checked the suspended bridges and found them to be satisfactory' - and had checked only the roof steel.
stakes: Whether the person whose seal is on the drawing is responsible for what happens after it leaves their desk. The Missouri Board said yes, and it cost two men their careers when no prosecutor would touch the case. For the viewer: everything they stand on was signed off by somebody, and the question of whether anyone actually looked is not rhetorical.
target_audience: English-speaking US general audience, with an unusually exact fit to PD's measured demographic - 93.4% male, 90.9% aged 55+, i.e. the people most likely to have built something, signed something off, or worked in a chain where each party assumed the next one had checked. This is the rare PD topic where the technical content is the emotional content for that viewer.

novelty_check.surfside_judgement: SAME FAMILY, NOT TOO CLOSE - but it is the nearest neighbour on the whole slate and it must be handled deliberately. Shared: a building, a mass-casualty collapse, a federal forensic investigation, an arithmetic of margins, and a country asking who is answerable. Different in the three ways that decide whether a viewer feels they have seen it before. (1) CAUSE: EP60 is decay and neglect over forty years - the building was already falling and everybody with a document said so. EP69 is a single decision at a single moment - the building was fine until one detail was changed and nobody recalculated. Slow rot versus one clean act. (2) ANSWER: EP60's investigation concluded in 2026, forty-five years after the building went up, and the film ends with margins that were 'too narrow from the start'. EP69's investigation was finished in ten months, the arithmetic is exact enough to put on screen as a bar chart, and the film can hand the viewer the whole causal chain in numbers they can check. (3) ENDING: EP60 ends with no accountability - no charges, a billion-dollar settlement, nobody answers. EP69 ends with two named professionals losing their licences in the first case of its kind in American engineering, on a legal standard - conscious indifference to a professional duty - that the tribunal had to invent for the occasion. A viewer who watched EP60 and then watches EP69 gets a different mechanism, a different epistemics and the opposite ending. That is a sequel, not a repeat. CONSTRAINTS THIS IMPOSES, BINDING: (a) do not schedule EP69 adjacent to EP60 - minimum four long-form slots apart; (b) EP69's hook must not reuse EP60's framing, its title shape, its thumbnail composition, or the word 'collapse' in the title if EP60's title uses it; (c) EP69's footage must not reuse EP60's clips - rubble, cranes, concrete, rescue, Florida coast - and the no-repeat check must be run across the two episodes together, not within EP69 alone; (d) EP69 leads with the DRAWING and the ROD, never with a building falling down. Note also that EP60's measured performance is currently uninformative (2 views at 3 days) and was correctly excluded from this judgement.
novelty_check.pinto_judgement: ADJACENT, NOT A CONFLICT, BUT SEQUENCING MATTERS. EP68 pinto is a design-defect-kills story and is being researched in a parallel thread right now. The two are structurally opposite and that is their value: Pinto is a company that knew and calculated and decided; Hyatt is a chain of professionals in which nobody calculated at all and each assumed another had. Do not ship them back to back, and do not let their thumbnails or titles rhyme.
novelty_check.titan_judgement: ADJACENT AND FAR ENOUGH. EP16 titan is a submersible, a private company, a safety culture that ignored warnings, and five deaths of people who chose to be there. EP69 is a building code, a state licensing statute, and 114 people who walked into a hotel lobby. No overlap in mechanism, jurisdiction, or visual vocabulary.

Heavily taught as an engineering-ethics case study, which means a large body of retellings that repeat the same secondary claims - the disputed telephone call above all - and a large audience that has met the story in a classroom and has never seen the arithmetic done properly.
differentiation: Almost every existing telling gets the load arithmetic approximately right and the provenance wrong. The most common failure, and the one this episode is built to avoid, is confusing NBS's 31 percent - a LOAD ratio, the load actually on the connection that night against the ultimate capacity the code expected - with a CAPACITY ratio. The Missouri Court of Appeals itself makes that slip in its footnote 12. This film gets it right, on screen, from the federal report's own sentences, and it can afford to because it has read the report. Second differentiator: the story is normally told as a whodunit about who changed the drawing, which is unanswerable and has never been determined. This film drops that and tells the answerable story instead - the review chain, in which the drawings told the fabricator the engineer had designed the connection while the engineer intended the fabricator to design it, and three parties stamped it. Third: it has an ending. The first American engineers to lose their licences for gross negligence, on a legal standard a tribunal had to invent, affirmed by a court in a published opinion that can be quoted.

visual_feasibility: Very high, and unusually well matched to PD's motion toolkit - this is the most buildable episode on the slate. The subject is five objects: a threaded rod, a welded box beam, a nut and washer, a line drawing, and a bar of load. All five are native FigureBeat/3D work with no likeness problem, no rights problem and no archive dependency. The centrepiece is already written by the record: the tribunal's finding was that the engineer did not assemble the connection's components to see what it looked like, so the film assembles it on screen in one continuous 3D move - it performs the act that was not performed. The binding shot vocabulary and a substitution table for every prohibited image are in section 12 of the facts ledger, so the designer does not improvise it.

risk_notes: MASS-CASUALTY EVENT WITH 114 DEAD. The hardest constraint on this episode is not factual, it is depiction. See ledger forbidden claims 10 to 14 and ledger section 12, which are binding.

NO THIRD-PARTY BROADCAST OR NEWS FOOTAGE. NONE. Not the KMBC TV videotape, not the Kansas City Star or Times photographs, not rescue footage, not a documentary clip, not blurred, not behind a graphic. This event is the single most tempting case on the slate for a violation because the collapse was filmed by a television crew who were in the room. Ledger forbidden claim 10.

NO GENERATED IMAGE MAY DEPICT A BODY, AN INJURED PERSON, A RESCUE, OR THE CROWDED LOBBY AT OR NEAR THE MOMENT OF COLLAPSE. The film may show the atrium filling at 3 p.m. and the atrium empty; it may not show the atrium full and then cut to the fall. Ledger forbidden claims 11 and 12, with a named replacement shot for every prohibited beat in ledger section 12.

NO VICTIM IS NAMED AND NO REAL PERSON'S LIKENESS APPEARS. Neither NBS nor the court names a single victim, so no selection problem arises - the film names none, and that is a decision, not an omission. Ledger forbidden claim 13.

TWO NAMED, POSSIBLY-LIVING ENGINEERS. Daniel M. Duncan and Jack D. Gillum were named publicly and disciplined by a state board. All criticism must rest on the Commission's findings as reproduced in 744 S.W.2d 524 and on NBS BSS 143, quoted, and nothing past them - no claim about knowledge, motive, character or finances. Ledger forbidden claims 15 and 17.
THEY WERE NEVER CRIMINALLY CHARGED. No charges were ever filed. Saying or implying otherwise throws away the ending, which is a licence revocation, not a conviction. Ledger forbidden claim 18.

THE LOAD ARITHMETIC IS THE FILM AND ONE NUMBER IS A TRAP. NBS's 31 percent is a LOAD ratio, not a CAPACITY ratio; the as-built capacity ratio is about 27 percent and is OUR arithmetic, never NBS's. The Missouri Court of Appeals itself conflates the two in its footnote 12, so that footnote must not be quoted for the engineering. Ledger forbidden claim 1.

THE DEATH TOLL MOVED. NBS in May 1982 counts 113; the Court of Appeals in 1988 and ASCE in 2000 say 114. Use 114 and cite the court. No retrieved document explains the gap and the film must not invent one. Ledger forbidden claim 3.

THE FAMOUS TELEPHONE CALL IS NOT IN THE OFFICIAL RECORD. The engineering-ethics teaching version - Havens rings G.C.E., someone approves, G.C.E. later denies the call - appears in neither the federal report nor the appellate opinion. Do not stage it. Ledger forbidden claim 5.

NO BLAME OUTSIDE THE FINDINGS. Havens Steel Company is a named company; the architect and contractor stamped the drawings but were never charged, and the Board chose not to investigate the architects at all. Ledger forbidden claim 16.

TIME-SENSITIVE. The most recent retrieved information about whether Duncan and Gillum are living dates from 1994-95. This must be re-checked at script lock and again before publish. Ledger open question 6.
